table.ruleA: Quarter or half: divide and round down (drop fraction). Melt is a whole number and never negative. All start BASE, slag 0, limit 38.
table.ruleB: Quarter or half of a mass: divide and round down. Mass is a whole number and never negative. All start LARVAL, waste 0, moult limit 38.
Holding limit, pupation mark, return mark, starting mass and feed schedule are identical figure for figure

table.ruleA: Add this cycle's row to each crucible. Working volume not enforced.
table.ruleB: Add this cycle's row to each chamber. Holding limit not enforced.

table.ruleA: Sequential 1 to 6. If melt > volume (strictly), the excess goes to the next crucible (already there before that crucible is handled) and the melt is set to the volume. Excess from 6 goes to slag.
table.ruleB: Sequential 1 to 6. If mass > limit (strictly), the excess goes to the next chamber (cascades) and the mass is set to the limit. Excess from 6 goes to waste.

table.ruleA: Read after Step 2. BASE and melt >= upper mark: becomes SUPERHEATED. SUPERHEATED and melt <= lower mark: becomes BASE. Otherwise unchanged. At most one change per cycle. Log (cycle, crucible, before, after).
table.ruleB: Read after step 2. LARVAL and mass >= pupation mark: becomes PUPAL. PUPAL and mass <= return mark: becomes LARVAL. Otherwise unchanged. At most one change per cycle. Log (cycle, chamber, before, after).

table.ruleA: Simultaneous. Every amount is computed from the melt at the start of the step and the state after Step 3: BASE takes floor(melt/4), SUPERHEATED takes floor(melt/2). Then all are applied at once. A BASE amount goes to slag. A SUPERHEATED amount goes to crucible n-1, or to slag if n=1. No volume cap.
table.ruleB: Sequential 1 to 6. Each amount is computed from the mass held at that moment and the stage after step 3: LARVAL takes floor(mass/4), PUPAL takes floor(mass/2). Each is applied immediately. A LARVAL amount goes to waste. A PUPAL amount goes to chamber n-1, or to waste if n=1. No limit cap.
table.difference: The wording differs (simultaneous vs sequential), but the function is the same. The only flow into chamber n in this step comes from chamber n+1, and chamber n+1 is handled after chamber n. So when B reaches chamber n, its mass still equals its start-of-step mass, and every amount matches A. Mass returned to n-1 lands after n-1 has been handled in both documents. This would differ only if B processed in the order 6 to 1.

table.ruleA: Sum all six. If the total > 38 (strictly; 38 does not fire), every crucible becomes floor(melt/2) and all removed melt goes to slag. Log the cycle.
table.ruleB: Sum all six. If the total > 38 (38 or less: nothing), every chamber becomes floor(mass/2) and all removed mass goes to waste. Log the cycle.

table.ruleA: (a) end melts 1 to 6, (b) end states, (c) all state changes, (d) tap cycles, (e) slag total, (f) balance: start + charges = end + slag
table.ruleB: (a) end masses 1 to 6, (b) end stages, (c) all stage changes, (d) moult cycles, (e) waste tally, (f) the same balance check

result.probeWhy: The only suspected difference is Step 4: A applies all amounts at once and B applies them one chamber at a time. The probe is built to stress that. Cycle 1 drives all six positions to SUPERHEATED/PUPAL at once, including position 1. That makes a chain of adjacent upstream returns, the case where a sequential pass and a simultaneous pass could split, and it also sends position 1's draw-off to the loss route. Every position starts at or above its working volume, so Step 2 cascades the full length of the line and spills off the end. The zero-input cycle and the alternating rows push melt down into the lower-mark band so states revert (cycles 2 and 3). The tap fires in 4 of the 5 cycles. As a supplement, a script ran 200,000 random start/input tables (values 0 to 9) through both documents and found 0 differences. All of those random runs happened to include at least one tap, so the no-tap path was not separately sampled; the structural argument covers it.
result.differingRule: None. The only difference is in wording. A's Step 4 is simultaneous and B's is sequential from 1 to 6. Because returns flow only upstream (n to n-1) and B processes downstream (1 to 6), no chamber receives a return before its own amount is computed. The two rules therefore give the same result for every input.
result.trust: The two routes agree. If they had disagreed, I would trust the table plus its structural argument over any single probe, because a probe only samples inputs.
